title: The talents (Matthew 25:14–30)
hook: two servants risk what they were given; the third buries his out of fear

segments.voice: Yesterday, workers in the vineyard: the five o'clock crew got a full day's pay, and the dawn crew grumbled. Your line was generosity isn't fair. it's better. Where did you catch yourself keeping score? Day twenty-nine.

A rich man is leaving on a long journey, and before he goes he calls in three servants and hands over his fortune. To the first, five talents. To the second, two. To the third, one. Each, the story says, according to his ability. Then he's gone. The first servant goes straight out and puts the money to work, trading, and doubles it. The second does the same and doubles his. The third walks out to a quiet spot, digs a hole, and buries his in the ground. Safe. Nobody can steal it. Nobody can lose it. A long time later the master comes home and calls them in to settle accounts. Two of them walk in with double. The third walks in with a shovel's worth of dirt still on the coins. Today's word is the thing they were given.
screen: `FIVE, TWO, ONE.` → `TWO PUT IT TO WORK.` → `ONE DIGS A HOLE.`

segments.voice: A talent was not a skill. It was a weight. In the ancient world a talent was a large weight of silver, worth something like twenty years of a laborer's wages. So even the one-talent servant was handed a fortune. And here's the part that sticks: our English word talent, meaning a gift or an ability, comes from this very parable. Centuries of Christians heard it, took the talents to mean the gifts God gives each person, and the word itself changed meaning. A story rewrote a dictionary. Now the moment it turns on. The first two walk in, and the master says the same thing to each, in the old King James Bible: "Well done, thou good and faithful servant." Then the third one speaks, and he's honest about why: "I was afraid, and went and hid thy talent in the earth." Afraid. He didn't waste it. He didn't steal it. He just couldn't bear the risk, so he buried it. And the ending is hard: his talent is taken and given away, and he's thrown out. Christians read this story in more than one way. Many hear it about gifts: whatever you've been given, however small, is meant to be used, not hidden. Others read it about waiting: it sits among Jesus's stories of the end of the age, and they hear a call to stay faithful until he comes back. And some readers notice that the third servant calls the master a hard man, reaping where he never sowed, and ask whether this master is meant to be God at all. Churches hold these readings side by side. What almost all of them share is the fear: the one thing the story won't praise is burying what you were given.
screen: `A TALENT WAS A WEIGHT OF SILVER.` · `A STORY REWROTE A DICTIONARY.` · `I WAS AFRAID, AND HID IT.` · `GIFTS, WAITING, OR A HARD MASTER?` · then, large: `WELL DONE, THOU GOOD AND FAITHFUL SERVANT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: find one gift you've been hiding. Settle, and breathe. Think of something you're good at, or used to be, that you've quietly put in the ground. Singing. Fixing things. Making people laugh. Listening. Writing. Don't argue with yourself about whether it counts. Just find it. Then ask what you were afraid of. Being bad at it. Being seen. If you pray, you can offer it back to God. If you don't, just hold it in your hands again for a minute. The bell holds the time.
Talent. A large weight of silver, entrusted to a servant. Because of this story, the English word came to mean a gift.
Your line: fear buries things. Today, dig one gift up and use it, even for five minutes, even badly, even where nobody sees. Day twenty-nine.

howItsDone: Many Christians read the parable of the talents as a call to use the gifts God has given them in service of others, and churches often preach on it when inviting people to volunteer or give.

fork.setup: you're the third servant. you've been handed one talent, a fortune, and your master is gone for a long time. what do you do?
options: trade with it and try to double it.
dig a hole and bury it where it's safe.
spend it and hope he never comes back.
fork.reveal: he buries it: "I was afraid, and went and hid thy talent in the earth." the story's hard ending falls on the one who played it safe.

original.note: Greek: a balance, and then a weight — the largest unit of silver money in the ancient world.

trapdoor: what you thought: a story about being talented.
what it means: three servants handed a fortune in silver. the one the story won't praise is the one who buried it out of fear.
what a scholar hears: talanton, a weight of silver worth years of wages. the English sense of talent, a gift, grew out of this parable.

notes: Value of a talent: commonly estimated at about 6,000 denarii, roughly twenty years of a laborer's wages; estimates vary. Confirm the phrasing 'something like twenty years'.
The English sense of 'talent' as natural ability is generally traced (via medieval Latin and French) to this parable; stated as fact. Confirm.

Three readings given without ranking: gifts; faithful waiting for Christ's return (the parable's setting in Matthew 24–25); and the minority reading that questions whether the harsh master stands for God (from 25:24). Confirm the third is fairly described and appropriate for this path.
The hard ending (25:28–30: talent taken, servant cast into outer darkness) is summarized as 'thrown out'; confirm.
Original: τάλαντον also meant a balance/scale; confirm the note.
